c.tagline: Andalusian soul of flamenco and orange blossom.

emergency.note: 091 reaches the National Police and 061 medical emergencies directly; 112 has English-speaking operators.

hood_landmark.Santa Cruz: the Real Alcázar palace beside the Cathedral and Giralda
hood_landmark.Triana: the Isabel II bridge and ceramic-tiled Triana Market on the Guadalquivir
hood_landmark.El Arenal: the Maestranza bullring and riverside Torre del Oro
hood_landmark.La Macarena: the Basílica de la Macarena and its revered Virgin
hood_landmark.Alameda: the Alameda de Hércules plaza with its Roman columns and bar terraces

avoid.reason: The Las Tres Mil Viviendas (Polígono Sur) housing estate in the south has serious crime and no tourist sights.
Pickpockets work Santa Cruz's lanes, the cathedral area and the packed Semana Santa and Feria crowds.

hood_desc: Santa Cruz is the atmospheric old Jewish quarter, a maze of whitewashed lanes and hidden plazas beside the Cathedral and Alcazar, ideal for first-timers who want to be in the postcard heart of the old town despite the crowds and tourist prices.

Triana sits across the river and keeps a proud working-class identity with ceramics workshops, flamenco roots, a lively food market and authentic tapas bars, suiting travelers who want local color and a neighborhood feel a short walk from the center.

El Arenal stretches between the Cathedral and the river around the Maestranza bullring, a central and slightly quieter area with classic tapas taverns and riverside strolls, good for those wanting a walkable base without the deepest tourist crush.

La Macarena is a genuine residential district to the north around its famous basilica, less touristy and more affordable with a bohemian, everyday Sevillano atmosphere, best for budget-minded visitors seeking local immersion.

Alameda, centered on the leafy Alameda de Hercules, is the hip, bohemian and LGBTQ-friendly hub with vintage shops, buzzing bars and the citys best nightlife, perfect for younger travelers who want energy after dark.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: Use the rechargeable Tarjeta Multiviaje, a TUSSAM/Metro smartcard sold at TUSSAM offices, metro machines and some kiosks (refundable deposit); contactless bank-card tap-to-pay is not yet accepted onboard. A single paper ticket costs about €1.40 (around $1.55), the Multiviaje card lowers each ride to roughly €0.69, and a 1-day tourist pass costs €5 (about $5.50).
transit.hours: Metro trains run about 6:30am to 11pm weekdays, extending to around 1-2am on Friday, Saturday and pre-holiday nights; buses and the tram keep similar hours, with a few night ("Búho") lines on weekends.
